passage: I'm Nilesh, and I don't like it when Tarun comes to lunch. He picks his nose and then his fingers go into his tiffin. Yesterday I wrinkled my nose and said, "Yuck, stop it!" and everyone laughed. Then Tarun said, "I don't want to sit here anymore," and moved away. I felt bad. My nose wrinkle was about the nose-picking, but it hurt him like it was about him. Tarun is sometimes alone at break. Today I told him quietly, "It's fine to sit here, but can you wash your hands first?" He nodded. I still find it gross, but I can be nice about it.

qa.q: What did Nilesh say when Tarun picked his nose at lunch?
qa.a: Nilesh said, "Yuck, stop it!"

qa.q: What did Nilesh feel after Tarun moved away, and why?
qa.a: Nilesh felt bad, because the disgust at the habit hurt Tarun as a person. Nilesh realised the yuck was meant for the habit, but Tarun took it personally.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do next time something a friend does feels disgusting?
qa.a: Nilesh can speak privately and kindly about the habit, like asking Tarun to wash first, without making Tarun feel unwelcome.

qa.q: How does Tarun likely experience being laughed at?
qa.a: Tarun probably felt embarrassed and rejected in front of everyone, so he moved away.

grounding: A child wrinkles their nose and says yuck, and learns disgust aimed at a person becomes exclusion, so kindness must be taught.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 4. At lunch today Darshan said "Yuck!" loudly about Madhav's fish curry and wrinkled his nose. Other children copied him and Madhav closed his lunchbox with a small face. I asked Darshan to step out with me and asked what he noticed about the smell. He said it was strong. I said that food he isn't used to can smell strange, but that our words can make someone feel unwelcome. Darshan looked at the floor and said he did not mean Madhav. I suggested that he tell Madhav so, and he did, adding, "Can I try a little?" Madhav nodded. I will watch how the two get on at lunch.

qa.q: What food did Madhav have at lunch?
qa.a: Madhav had fish curry.

qa.q: What might Darshan have been feeling when he said he did not mean Madhav, and what else could it show?
qa.a: He may have felt guilty and embarrassed once he realised the yuck hurt Madhav. It could also show he was reacting to the smell without thinking of the person.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to build kindness in the class after this?
qa.a: The teacher could talk about respecting different foods and encourage children to say "I'm not used to that" instead of "yuck".

qa.q: How might Madhav feel after Darshan asks to try a little?
qa.a: Madhav might feel relieved and included, since he nodded, though he might also still feel a little hurt from earlier.

grounding: A child says yuck at a smell; disgust aimed at a person becomes exclusion, so a teacher helps teach kindness.

passage:
Friday
Today at lunch, Shankar opened his tiffin and it was bitter gourd. I said, "Yuck!" and wrinkled my nose. It smelled so strong.
Then Priyanka said, "Shankar smells like bitter gourd," and everyone moved their tiffins away from him. Shankar closed his box and didn't eat.
I felt terrible. My "yuck" started it. It was about the food, not about him. But the others made it about him.
After lunch I told Shankar, "Sorry. I don't like bitter gourd, but you're not yuck." He shrugged but gave a small smile.
Tomorrow I'll sit next to him.
- Ishita

qa.q: What was in Shankar's tiffin?
qa.a: Bitter gourd.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling after the others moved away from Shankar?
qa.a: Ishita felt guilty and sorry, realising the "yuck" about food had turned into excluding Shankar.

qa.q: What did Ishita do to make it right?
qa.a: Ishita apologised to Shankar, explaining the dislike was about the food, not him, and planned to sit next to him.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt when everyone moved away?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and embarrassed, left out because of his food.

grounding: A child's diary shows disgust at food turning into exclusion of a person, and choosing kindness instead.

passage:
At the village fair, Saurabh walked past the fish stall and pinched his nose. "Yuck! It stinks!"
Arohi, who was cleaning fish at her family's stall, heard him. She bent her head lower and scrubbed faster.
Saurabh's grandmother, walking with him, stopped. "Saurabh, the smell is strong, yes. But look at her hands. She's working hard to help her family."
Saurabh looked. Arohi's fingers were red from the cold water.
He felt his face go hot. He walked over. "Sorry. The fish smells, but you're not yucky."
Arohi looked up, surprised, and nodded.
On the way home, Saurabh asked his grandmother, "Can we buy fish from her next time?"

qa.q: What did Saurabh do when he passed the fish stall?
qa.a: He pinched his nose and said, "Yuck! It stinks!"

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she bent her head and scrubbed faster?
qa.a: Arohi probably felt embarrassed and hurt by Saurabh's words.

qa.q: How did Saurabh's grandmother help him?
qa.a: She agreed the smell was strong but pointed out Arohi's hard work, teaching him to separate disgust at smells from how he treats people.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's grandmother see his apology?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and relieved that Saurabh noticed Arohi's hard work and turned a careless yuck into kindness.

grounding: At a village fair, a child's disgust at a smell becomes hurtful to a person, and his grandmother teaches kindness.

passage:
In the school canteen in Oslo, Anders opened his lunchbox and the smell of pickled herring filled the table. Bilal wrinkled his nose. "Eww!"
Others joined in. "Fishy Anders! Fishy Anders!"
Anders shut the box and sat very still.
Bilal suddenly remembered last year, when he brought biryani and someone called it "stinky rice." He remembered how his face burned.
He turned to the others. "Stop. It's just food. I didn't like it, but that doesn't mean we tease him."
Then he said to Anders, "What does it taste like?"
Anders shrugged. "Sour. And a bit sweet."
Bilal took a tiny bite. His face twisted. Anders laughed. "Told you it's sour!"

qa.q: What was in Anders's lunchbox?
qa.a: Pickled herring.

qa.q: Why did Bilal decide to stop the teasing?
qa.a: He remembered feeling embarrassed and hurt when others called his biryani "stinky rice," so he felt empathy for Anders.

qa.q: What did Bilal do that was kind?
qa.a: He told the others to stop, separated disliking food from teasing a person, and showed interest in Anders's food.

qa.q: How might Anders feel after Bilal tasted the herring?
qa.a: Anders probably felt relieved and included, laughing together instead of being teased.

grounding: In a school canteen, a child's disgust at food nearly becomes exclusion, and he chooses kindness.

passage: In the school canteen, Tanvir pinched his nose. "Yuck! What's that smell?" Noor slowly closed the lid of her tiffin; it held dried-fish curry, her Nani's recipe. Two boys slid their trays away from her. Noor stared at the table. Mr Bose, on lunch duty, came and sat opposite them. "Tanvir, your nose is allowed to dislike a smell. What's not okay is making Noor feel she has to hide her food." Tanvir looked at Noor's lowered head and his face went red. "I didn't mean her. Just the smell." "Then tell her that." Tanvir mumbled, "Sorry. It's just strong for me." Noor lifted the lid a little. "It's strong for everyone. It's still the best." Tanvir laughed, and the boys slid their trays back.

qa.q: Who was on lunch duty?
qa.a: Mr Bose.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's face go red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and sorry once he saw Noor's lowered head and understood that his 'yuck' had landed on her, not just on the smell.

qa.q: What did Mr Bose teach that could help next time?
qa.a: That disliking a smell is fine, but aiming disgust at a person shuts them out, so Tanvir should talk about the smell and apologise to Noor directly.

qa.q: What was it like for Noor when the boys slid their trays away?
qa.a: Noor likely felt ashamed and shut out, as if her family's food made her unwelcome.

grounding: It illustrates a child's nose-wrinkling disgust at a smell spilling into exclusion of a classmate, and an adult teaching the difference with kindness.
